channel.title: Tangle - the good parts
channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The protests and riots in France.
item.dc:creator: Ari Weitzman
item.description: Plus, moonshine before the Supreme Court.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The protests in France. For the past month, protests and riots have broken out across France, with violence and disorder significantly escalating over the weekend. In mid-September, high school students began demonstrating against a perceived lack of resources in schools; parents, college students, teachers and trade unions later joined the effort, and it has since broadened into nationwide unrest over cost-of-living concerns. French officials say that far-left groups are primarily responsible for the escalation into rioting and looting, while some French politicians and U.S. political leaders suggest the protests underscore deeper issues linked to immigration. 

Back up: The protests began in Paris-area schools, where students and parents have highlighted overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, aging infrastructure, and a lack of investment in the education system. By early October, several violent incidents led to hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries, as well as significant property damage. French officials claim that “ultra-left” groups, such as La France Insoumise, have catalyzed the violence and want to encourage chaos ahead of France’s 2027 elections. Right-wing politicians have argued that heightened levels of immigration and government tolerance of disorder have fueled the riots.

On Saturday, an estimated 550,000–800,000 protesters participated in 110 marches across France, and many demonstrations resulted in clashes between participants and police. Officials say approximately 1,000 law enforcement officers and firefighters were injured, 2,400 people were arrested, and 3,000 businesses were damaged. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said police “had lost control” and suggested he would impose a national state of emergency if necessary. In a national address, French President Emmanuel Macron said, “Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.” Paris police issued a partial curfew Monday night. 

Some protesters have criticized the police response as overly aggressive, highlighting an incident where a 15-year-old student lost his hand from a police stun grenade. Many politicians, pundits and citizens have condemned the vandalism and rioting, though some protesters have defended it. “The state is violent and property damage is the people’s response to that violence,” one college student protester said. “The violence in the streets is against property, not people.” 

On Monday, President Donald Trump linked the riots to immigration, writing on Truth Social, “The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” On X, Vice President JD Vance said, “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen.”

Today, we’ll have views from the left, right and French writers on the protests and riots, followed by Managing Editor Ari Weitzman’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left is mixed, with some suggesting the U.S. is similarly ripe for protest. 
  • Others question whether protests will address France’s underlying issues.

In The Philadelphia Inquirer, Will Bunch asked “do French protests have a message for America?”

“In recent years, billions of dollars in badly needed maintenance have been postponed, resulting in classrooms with toxic hazards like asbestos and ancient lead paint, stale, polluted air, inadequate heat in winter, and a lack of air-conditioning in summer,” Bunch wrote. “These, of course, are the K-12 conditions in the Philadelphia School District, and school squalor like this is something you see in a lot of large American cities, unfortunately.”

“But while there’s the occasional one-off rally… we’ve seen nothing when it comes to protesting like what’s happening this month in France,” Bunch said. “Unless you follow the big international news sites, the youth protests in France and India haven’t received extensive media coverage here in the U.S. You could argue that’s because we have plenty of our own problems on American soil… Which brings back the question: Why isn’t America’s Gen Z manning the barricades?”

The Economist argued “no one is addressing the core problems the country faces.”

“The context for the riots is the underlying tension linked to next year’s election… The country wants change, but is deeply divided about what should come next,” the writer said. “It looks probable that the polarisation of public debate and the politicisation of the street will intensify over the next six months — and probably beyond… [If Le Pen wins in 2027,] it could prompt a new round of protests on the left.”

“The government’s budget deficit is expected to be 5.4% of GDP this year, one of the highest in the euro zone,” the writer said. “Wariness in the markets and anger on the streets make for a toxic mix. Worse, as attention turns to law and order, France is even less likely to have the political conversation it badly needs: about what sort of welfare system it can afford and how to generate the wealth needed to sustain it.”

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right worry ascendant ideologies in the U.S. could prompt similar protests. 
  • Others note the electoral factors affecting France’s protests.

In The Daily Signal, Steve Cortes said “Europe is burning — is America next?”

“A violent weekend of Marxist-Islamist protests rocked Europe, from Portugal to Italy. The worst carnage erupted across France, where rioters torched the revered, architecturally stunning town hall of Limoges. The 143-year-old landmark is a protected national monument. Its roof caved in, and its iconic bell tower collapsed into the flames,” Cortes wrote. “Is this kind of mayhem headed to America next?

“Sadly, current trends suggest that the growing ‘red-green’ alliance of hardcore leftists and radical Islamists in the United States could produce exactly this kind of disorder and destruction here, if we are not vigilant — and if the looming elections go poorly for nationalist candidates,” Cortes said. “Admittedly, [Marxist and Islamist] political factions make a strange political marriage, and they clearly disagree on many topics, especially social issues. So, what binds this dangerous new merger? A common enemy. They both hate Western civilization.”

The Wall Street Journal editorial board described “why France is burning.”

“The news this time is the pre-election play by far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” the board wrote. “The riots are ostensibly about declining public services, but the presidential election next April figures into the protest calculations… If the riots move more center-right voters away from the centrist candidates and toward Ms. Le Pen, Mr. Mélenchon may figure he has a fighting chance to become the next President in the May runoff.”

“The parties of the right and left see a rare opportunity to use the moment to gain the Élysée Palace,” the board said. “As a lame duck, [Macron] is left to rely on police to protect the French streets. They couldn’t do it on Saturday, as protesters ransacked shops in Marseille and elsewhere, and even torched the historic town hall in Limoges that survived the Nazis. France is in a violent democratic funk, and it will probably get worse. Don’t think it can’t happen in the U.S. given the current state of American politics.”

What writers in France are saying.
  • Some say the unrest is a response to President Macron’s failures.
  • Others criticize protesters for fomenting chaos.

The Le Monde editorial board said the protests “force Macron to confront the failures of his presidency.”

“Saturday’s protests should not be reduced to these acts of looting and destruction. French President Emmanuel Macron emphasized this in an address on Sunday evening,” the board wrote. “Yet, for the past 10 years, Macron has consistently turned a deaf ear to the social movements that have marked his two terms. Refusing compromise, his successive governments have systematically bypassed unions since 2017, contributing to their weakening. 

“By doing so, the authorities have deprived themselves of the essential intermediaries needed to channel public anger. Meanwhile, Macron has distanced himself from the youth by pushing unpopular reforms and ignoring their growing discontent,” the board said. “Listening to and respecting dialogue partners is essential. But above all, the government must give concrete political responses to their demands, which it can no longer afford to reject out of hand. Social peace can only be restored under these conditions.”

In The Free Press, Simone Rodan-Benzaquen called protesters’ actions “an assault on democracy.”

“The government needs to protect officials and teachers, prosecute their attackers, and get schools open. It needs to investigate police abuses seriously, without accepting that those abuses justify an assault on anyone in uniform,” Rodan-Benzaquen wrote. “I believe in the French Republic. I resent the suggestion that caring about its survival makes someone naive, or secretly authoritarian. We have the right to protest because we live in a democracy.

“We also have the right to go to school, to disagree with a crowd, and to elect a mayor who can do the job without fearing for his family,” Rodan-Benzaquen said. “Marseille’s city hall is not the Bastille. The people who broke into it were not staging a just revolution against authoritarianism; they were attacking the means by which their fellow citizens govern themselves… I want a government that understands how serious this is — and acts before another public servant, or another family, pays the price.”

My take.
Ari Weitzman
Managing Editor
 
 
  • The disorder in France is downstream of a few straightforward issues that have been building for some time.
  • More complicated factors are at play, too, prompting uncomfortable but necessary discussions about changes to French society.
  • Ultimately, France has a tough balance to strike between over-correction and not responding strongly enough.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

It’s tempting to tell a simple, three-part story about these protests and stop there.  

Part one of the simple story starts in the French suburb of Créteil, where students began protesting a lack of school resources. Protests are a fixture of French culture; as recently as 2018–2020, “Yellow Vest protesters” flooded the streets to demand the government address rising gas prices and weakening economic opportunities for workers.

A more recent fixture has been a forceful police response. In 2017, France passed a law allowing police to use weapons for reasons other than self-defense. Since then, French law enforcement has increased its use of non-lethal weapons against protesters, particularly guns that fire rubber pellets (called “lanceur de balles de défense,” or LBDs). Authorities said they needed to take stronger measures to respond to violent elements who commingle with protesters. 

Whatever the cause, the effect has been dramatic. Eye injuries caused by LBDs increased from two in 2016 and one in 2017 to 25 in 2018 and 15 in part of 2019. The sudden increase led to a rebuke from Europe’s human rights commissioner, who said France’s policing tactics against the Yellow Vest protesters were making it a violent outlier from the rest of Europe. 

That context is crucial to understanding part two, the tipping point that intensified the past month’s protests. In late September, the student-led protests spread from the Parisian suburbs to cities across France. On September 30, a 16-year-old was blinded in his right eye by injuries that prosecutors described as consistent with an LBD. Then, on October 5, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off by a police grenade.

This incident ushered in part three, as at least 160,000 teachers and parents joined the marches. Protests spread across Europe. The Yellow Vests joined the movement. Then, rioting and looting broke out in French cities over the weekend — rioters burned a tourist office in Lyon, set fire to the 143-year-old town hall in Limoges, and looted Marseille’s city center. By Monday morning, at least 3,000 storefronts had been vandalized, and looters in Marseille were brazenly gathering their spoils in broad daylight.

In the simple story, a protest about something specific began attracting dissatisfied factions, particularly from the left, who were more bent on destruction and crime than delivering a political message (and who actually undermined the original message the students were raising). But that narrative doesn’t tell the whole story. Instead, the whole story asks you to confront an uncomfortable element that is easy to discern the moment you start watching videos, listening to eyewitnesses, or reading local accounts.

Right-wing commenter Thaïs d’Escufon presented this element as strongly as possible in two contrasting videos. In the first, a white woman is pleading with the mob not to loot a nearby store, saying “this isn’t for the cause” as she is gently held back by a member of the crowd. In the second, a Muslim business owner trying to protect her storefront is aided by members of the crowd, who tell looters “don’t smash it up, she’s a sister” and “it’s okay, my brothers, please go.”

As French writer Charles Consigny bluntly stated on a daily French talk show, “the looters are children of immigrants.” Frankly, I’m having a hard time processing that claim — because I’m finding more reason to support it than to reject it. On the same show, a caller who identified herself as a Muslim business owner whose shop had been looted in Marseille said, “It’s unfortunate, but 80% — it’s my community.” Additionally, a police union representative said most of the looters were from “disadvantaged neighborhoods,” outlying communities like Créteil that are often home to immigrant families.

Conversely, the response that Green Party MP Sandrine Rousseau gave to Consigny was a passionate plea not to blame immigrants for the damage, saying immigrants are part of the fabric of French culture and many are firefighters and police responding to the destruction. Rousseau is right, almost obviously so: Most immigrant families are law-abiding citizens who contribute to the societies of their adopted home countries. However, Rousseau notably didn’t deny Consigny’s central claim, which is somewhat telling. I’m not willing to go as far as to say that the rioting in Marseille is proof of “migrant chaos” causing “Europe’s decline,” but as of this moment, I have more reason to believe Consigny than I do to dismiss him. So, if it’s true that many of the looters were children of immigrants, why is that the case?

I think that question has a scary answer that I’m hesitant to agree with and an easy answer that doesn’t tell us much. The hard answer is what Steve Cortes wrote in The Daily Signal (under “What the right is saying”), that these looters are representative of a tide of migrants who hate Western civilization but are increasingly seeking refuge in Western civilization. The easy answer is simply that the rioters and looters come from poor families, who tend to disproportionately be immigrant families, and their rioting and looting is largely an economic impulse. 

Grappling with these answers is very uncomfortable and difficult for me. I generally tend towards accepting the easy answer, but I’m aware of how, well, easy it is. I also don’t think the civilizational concern should just be dismissed out of hand, especially as French social media is awash with videos reposting a 1979 speech by Ayatollah Khomeini over images of rioting and destruction in France from this past weekend. The ‘red–green’ alliance between communist protesters and Islamist extremists that Cortes described feels meaningful to me, as does the paucity of the responses to this criticism from the left. 

Frankly, I don’t know how anyone can deny that the communist/Islamist rhetoric coming from these protesters is oppositional towards Western civilization. However, I have a much harder time accepting that young students calling themselves communists or online posters calling for an anti-Western jihad are the same people smashing up a Hermès store to sell handbags online. I’ve spent plenty of time on college campuses — the people espousing the most extreme rhetoric are often not at all willing to back it up with correspondingly extreme actions, instead opting for more milquetoast public disruptions. I ultimately believe that the worst of the weekend’s riots came from low-brow opportunists, the same kind of people who look for excuses to steal, smash and burn that we’ve seen time and time again, in the U.S. and abroad.

France is now tasked with drawing a line between protecting its long-practiced ability to demonstrate publicly and punishing crimes committed during those demonstrations. As of today, it’s pushing back against the resale of stolen goods and instigating curfews, while politicians from the left are themselves pushing back against the crackdown as collective punishment. If France goes too far in its enforcement, it risks its own culture of protests and citizen trust in the government. But if it doesn’t go far enough, it will not only send a permissive signal to opportunists who came out under the cover of protests, but to the red–green alliance itself. It’s a delicate moment, and if the French government gets this wrong, the circumstances could be dire and long-lasting.

Staff dissent.
Audrey Moorehead
Editor
 
 
I understand Ari’s desire to differentiate between online agitators whose rhetoric doesn’t translate into action and the opportunists who use civil unrest as an excuse to loot and burn, but I ultimately find it misguided.
 
Ideological opposition to the West is an ever-present problem in France, Europe at large, and even the United States. Some of this opposition is homegrown, coming from lifelong Westerners who have become enraptured with visions of a secular, utopian communist future (usually leftist agitators) or with romanticizations of a white Christian pastoral age gone by (usually rightist agitators). But some of this radicalism is brought in from elsewhere, by immigrants who seek the economic opportunities of the West without embracing the culture that produced those opportunities.
 
And to Ari’s point, most of these agitators are just blowhards; X’s Nazi propagandists and Bluesky’s Mao apologists are not necessarily the ones throwing bricks through store windows. But the normalization of opposition to the West creates the conditions for violence: It motivates people to look the other way from looting and burning, or even to permit looting and burning in service of broader goals. So while these French protests aren’t going to be the killing blow that starts the revolution, they’re another brick through a window of Western civilization; and the people inside the building are becoming less and less likely to want to patch it up.
 
If we admit that we must combat anti-Western radicalism, we have to think about how to do it. Combating homegrown radicalism, which is usually borne out of misunderstandings of the Western tradition, is difficult — it requires being more intentional about presenting the tradition’s past and its desired future. But combating imported radicalism has an easier solution: It requires revisiting immigration policies and examining whether a stopper on immigration, in order to better assimilate extant migrant populations, might be useful.

Take the survey: What’s driving the protests and riots? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

Under the radar.

On Monday, the Supreme Court announced that it will hear a challenge to an 1868 federal law that bans the production of spirits like bourbon and whiskey at personal residences. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit previously found the ban unconstitutional, but the federal government appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that at-home production allows individual producers to avoid inspections and taxes. The Hobby Distillers Association, the main group challenging the law, says that the ban exceeds Congress’s taxation power. Oral arguments are expected in early 2027. SCOTUSblog has the story.

item.title: Could Texas turn blue?
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Ken Paxton and James Talarico are in a nail-biter.
item.content:encoded:
My rule for writing about Texas politics is pretty simple: I work under the assumption that it is a red state until that assumption stops being correct. The one time I deviated from the strategy, I got it woefully wrong.

I never got too worked up about the possibility that Beto O’Rourke, MJ Hegar, or Colin Allred could rewrite electoral maps. I won’t overestimate Talarico’s odds here, either, despite how unpopular President Trump is, or how bad of a candidate Paxton is, or how neck-and-neck this race seems.

Still, both candidates’ cases for victory are pretty easy to craft. Let’s start with the case for why Talarico is going to win:

President Trump is historically unpopular. Gasoline prices are high and diesel prices are through the roof, which is going to hurt Trump in a state with many long-haul drivers and pickup trucks. The president won Texas by 14 points in 2024, supported in large part by the Latino vote and anti-Kamala Harris sentiment. Now, Latinos are shifting back to the left, Democrats have a much stronger candidate on the ballot and we’re in a midterm election, which historically hurts the incumbent party. The closest analogue here might be the 2018 midterm race, when Trump was in office and O’Rourke came within 2.6 points of flipping Ted Cruz’s Senate seat, despite polls showing him much further behind. These races come down to turnout, and Democrats seem much more committed to voting than Republicans do this election season. 

Speaking of Republicans, Ken Paxton is a disaster. He’s a comically corrupt (alleged) adulterer, in a national environment where voters say corruption is their number-one issue and in a state where traditional marital values are popular. Leaks from Paxton’s campaign portray a candidate who knows Trump is hurting him and can’t find his footing on the trail.

On paper, all the momentum and evidence look good for Talarico. While O’Rourke made noise, he never led a single poll; Talarico has had an advantage in the polls since August and is running in a much more favorable environment. Plus, the concocted conspiracy theory that Talarico was checked into a mental health facility reeks of desperation. If it weren’t for Elon Musk floating Paxton’s campaign, Talarico’s historic fundraising numbers would be a giant advantage and a huge story. In southwest Texas, the administration’s attempt to build a border wall in the Big Bend region and National Park is activating huge blowback from a bipartisan coalition of politicians, ranchers, hunters, river guides, small business owners, and even law enforcement. And while Trump accused Talarico of avoiding a debate, the reality is Talarico’s campaign has repeatedly tried to organize a debate with Paxton, and Paxton keeps dodging him — so much so that Talarico ended up doing a solo town hall with Texas voters that was aired on CNN last Wednesday. 

Anecdotally, I’d add that Talarico’s campaign has a tremendous amount of enthusiasm among Democrats in Texas. I live in New Jersey full time but own property in West Texas, where I spent my summers growing up and now spend a lot of my winters. I’ve never felt anything like the current political momentum there, and it’s all going in one direction: an all-out effort to oust Gov. Greg Abbott (R), stop Ken Paxton, and rein in President Trump.

Get more of the story...
We broke down the race with just the facts, and then we picked out the best arguments from conservative, progressive, and independent writers in today's free newsletter so you can make up your own mind. Read them here. 

For Democrats, that all sounds pretty exciting. But the case for Paxton is still compelling.

At baseline, Texas is a red state. The state doesn’t collect party registration data, but Trump’s decisive victory in 2024 is one of the best measures of how voters break in statewide elections. A recent YouGov survey has 41% of likely voters in Texas identifying as Republican, 26% as Democrat, and 28% as independent — close, but still a healthy Republican advantage. 

Meanwhile, the core issues that are driving Trump’s unpopularity — the war in Iran, affordability, and the immigration crackdown — are all softened in Texas. Yes, diesel prices are high nationally, and Texas has faced its own economic emergency over those costs. But unlike other states, Texas also has an upside from the war: Its oil production is thriving, meaning Texas producers can charge more, juice profits, and provide a lot of jobs. Trump’s nationally unpopular mass-deportation effort has a lot of support in Texas. And Trump, who is still good at turning out his base, has spent a lot of political capital throwing his weight behind Paxton.

And then there’s Musk. With nearly $160 million spent already, he’s single-handedly funding super PACs that are blanketing the state in pro-Paxton or anti-Talarico ads. And, if you watched the CNN town hall, voters were more focused on Talarico’s progressive social views (some from as recently as 2020 and 2021) than on his populist left economic views, which is a problem for his campaign. We’ve seen that focus on progressive social views work for the GOP before, and Republican groups are even running the same “He is for they/them” ad against Talarico that was famously effective against Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race. As I detailed in my latest YouTube video, fear is a powerful and effective campaign strategy, one Texas Republicans are deploying to a much higher degree than Talarico in this cycle (they even have AI-generated ads of Talarico defacing a Bible).

Finally, the “closeness” of the race could be a total mirage, anyway. In 2024, polling showed Trump with a roughly seven-point lead and he won by 14. In that year’s Senate race, polls showed Cruz up about four points on Colin Allred; he won by over eight points. In the 2022 governor’s race, Abbott led O’Rourke by an average of eight points; he won by about 11. 

Which is all just to say that the polling may be tight (and point to a Talarico advantage), but I have less confidence in current polls than I have in a long time. I’m holding off on any midterm predictions until we get closer to Election Day, but this race obviously has the potential to tilt the Senate map — and make Texas history. 

Moved by the take? Share it!

item.title: The Texas Senate race.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, who enforces constitutional anti-corruption rules?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Texas Senate race. With approximately two weeks until the midterm elections, state Rep. James Talarico (D) and state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) are in a tightly contested race that could determine control of the Senate. Recent financial disclosures show that Elon Musk has given nearly $160 million to support Paxton, while Talarico announced his campaign raised $64 million in Q3 2026. Early voting in Texas begins on Monday.

Back up: Talarico and Paxton are running to replace Sen. John Cornyn (R), who Paxton defeated in the Republican Senate primary. No Democrat has won a statewide office in Texas since 1994.

Campaign finance filings released last week revealed that Musk has donated $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, Senate Republicans’ primary super PAC, which has sent the money to Texas PAC, a group supporting Paxton (Musk has given more through other groups). Separately, Talarico’s $64 million Q3 fundraising is the largest third-quarter fundraising ever by a Senate candidate. Talarico has raised $134.3 million in total to date. Overall advertising spending on the race recently surpassed $500 million.

An October CBS News poll found Talarico with a 51%–49% lead over Paxton among likely voters. Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball and Cook Political Report both rate the race as a toss-up after classifying it as “lean Republican” earlier in the campaign.

On Friday, October 9, Talarico resumed public campaigning after a nearly two-week absence while sick with the flu. His campaign said he began feeling ill after a September 29 fundraiser in New York, went to urgent care when he returned to Texas, then spent the beginning of October recovering at home. After Paxton and others began questioning his absence, conservative accounts on X promoted a claim that he was at a mental health facility in Ohio. The facility denied that Talarico had ever visited, and The New York Times confirmed that security footage from outside Talarico’s home showed he had been at his residence during his absence. 

Separately, Paxton has been criticized for alleged ethical violations, including a 2015 indictment for securities fraud and whistleblower complaints of bribery and abuse of office, for which he was impeached by the Texas state House. On Monday, October 12, The Wall Street Journal shared video of Paxton at a 2024 New Year’s Eve celebration in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, alongside two men wanted in the U.S. for healthcare fraud and a woman believed to be his mistress. “Like President Trump, Ken Paxton has been politically persecuted for years,” Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux said in response to the story. “Every time, voters have seen through it and sent him back to office because they know he has always fought for Texas.”

Below are views from the right, left, and writers in Texas on the Senate race. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right say Talarico is trying — and failing — to conceal past progressive positions.
  • Others suggest Republicans could lose the seat.

In The American Spectator, Buck Throckmorton wrote “Talarico’s political reversals stir trouble in Texas Senate race.”

“Shortly before his disappearance [from the campaign trail,] Mr. Talarico embraced the ‘Trust me, I’m lying’ strategy regarding several of his previous radical positions, trying to temporarily position himself in the mainstream on issues such as sex-change surgery for minors,” Throckmorton said. “This is a fraught strategy that rarely works any longer. It comes across as pandering dishonesty to the moderates he is appealing to, while it is simultaneously received as betrayal by activists who will not tolerate political dissimulation.”

“It will take a near-perfect confluence of events for Talarico to eke out a victory. Disregarding the historic Democrat bias of the polls involved, Talarico would need massive Democrat turnout… [He] also must somehow capture a great many crossover Republican voters,” Throckmorton wrote. “There are not many Trump 2024 / Talarico 2026 voters, but that is what Talarico must have in great numbers.”

In The Washington Examiner, Abigail Ingram argued “Republicans are to blame” if Talarico wins.

“Talarico’s platform is simple. Elites are greedy, and good-hearted people are suffering as a result… Both the GOP and Democratic National Committee have, at times, employed similar messaging to appeal to well-intended voters. What is surprising is the response from Paxton,” Ingram said. “Paxton’s platform focuses, in large part, on the radicalism of his opponent’s political party. His would-be voters are confronted with one ask: keep Texas the same. 

“But by campaigning on opposition to progress, Paxton might be inadvertently shooting himself in the foot,” Ingram wrote. “Texas Republicans are falling prey to the very same trap that doomed Democrats during the federal election in 2024… The DNC banked on widespread antipathy toward Donald Trump to keep itself in the White House. Americans lived through the alleged fluke that was Trump’s first presidential term. They would never willingly choose a redo — right? Wrong.”

What the left is saying.
  • Some on the left are cautiously optimistic about Talarico’s chances.
  • Others criticize the forces that elevated the Talarico mental health story.

In USA Today, Sara Pequeño wrote “polls are shouting in favor of Talarico in Texas. We'll see.”

“As we have learned time and again, polls aren’t always trustworthy. But one thing is clear: Talarico is moving the needle in a state known as a GOP stronghold. Even if we don’t know the outcome yet, it’s clear that he’s making Republicans sweat in a state they normally wouldn’t worry about,” Pequeño said. “The seminarian and member of the state House of Representatives is delivering a message of hope and progress, one that Texas Democrats have longed to hear for years now.”

“In some ways, this Texas Senate race feels like a repeat of the matchup between Republican Sen. Ted Cruz and former Democratic Rep. Beto O’Rourke in 2018. O’Rourke drummed up a lot of national media attention, only to lose by 2.6 points,” Pequeño wrote. “Talarico is polling better than O’Rourke did, while Trump is polling worse than he was in 2018. It doesn’t mean that Talarico is destined to win — I don’t think anybody believes that, even Democrats — but it’s clear that he has a shot. Republicans certainly seem to think so.”

In Salon, Sophia Tesfaye said “a viral Talarico hoax drowned out Paxton’s corruption story.”

“Right-wing influencers invented a story that Talarico had secretly checked into an Ohio psychiatric facility, and the search traffic around the Democrat exploded. The lie collapsed with almost embarrassing speed, and the people who spread it now face potential legal exposure,” Tesfaye wrote. “By the time the story fell apart, the damage had already been done… a Republican politician facing serious questions about his own conduct had been handed a convenient distraction.”

“The only people who benefit from a manufactured outrage are the people selling it and the politicians who can hide behind it,” Tesfaye said. “And hide is precisely what Paxton needed to do. On Monday the Wall Street Journal reported that only days after being indicted for embezzlement, a fugitive donated $25,000 to the attorney general… [The story] was buried under a fabricated tale about his opponent’s mental health.”

What writers in Texas are saying.
  • Some writers note Talarico’s positions are constantly shifting.
  • Others say Texans should reject Paxton.

In Texas Scorecard, Kenny Webster described “the tale of two Talaricos.”

“There appear to be two James Talaricos, and they do not always agree with each other… One of them says he’s against Big Tech, the other voted to give subsidies to data centers and takes money from Silicon Valley billionaires,” Webster wrote. “One of them says fossil fuels are destroying the planet and the Texas oil-and-gas industry is like cassette tapes that aren’t going to last, the other says he’ll protect oil-and-gas jobs and stand up to his own party if they mess with the industry.”

“[Talarico] stated that modern science recognizes six biological sexes. He opposed measures that would have required athletes to compete according to biological sex and called the concern manufactured,” Webster said. “The new Talarico now running statewide maintains that there are two sexes, that he would support a national ban on surgeries for minors, and that he opposes transgender athletes in girls’ sports when safety or fairness is endangered.”

The San Antonio Express-News editorial board argued “Talarico offers Texans a chance to choose integrity for U.S. Senate.”

“The choice before voters is ethical and moral, not merely political,” the board wrote. “Talarico is a Democrat through and through, and yet given the dynamics of this race, he is also a far more fitting successor to longtime Republican U.S. Sen. John Cornyn… Talarico brings a new brand of optimism in the form of a youthful former public school teacher who wears his Christian faith on his sleeve without feeling compelled to wipe it on others.”

“He is arguing Texans are more alike than they are different, and the most existential struggle in the Texas Legislature and U.S. Congress is not between Democrats and Republicans but rather between the top and the bottom,” the board said. “In Paxton, voters have one of the most breathtakingly flawed, immoral, cynical and ethically challenged candidates ever to run in a Texas statewide race… He has shown little regard for democracy, suing to overturn the 2020 presidential election and wasting millions of dollars to prosecute nonexistent voter fraud.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • The case for Talarico winning is strong — Democrats have momentum and he’s consistently led the polls.
  • However, Paxton has an equally strong case: Polling is unreliable and Republicans don’t lose in Texas.
  • I expect this race to go right down to the wire.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

My rule for writing about Texas politics is pretty simple: I work under the assumption that it is a red state until that assumption stops being correct. The one time I deviated from the strategy, I got it woefully wrong.

I never got too worked up about the possibility that Beto O’Rourke, MJ Hegar, or Colin Allred could rewrite electoral maps. I won’t overestimate Talarico’s odds here, either, despite how unpopular President Trump is, or how bad of a candidate Paxton is, or how neck-and-neck this race seems.

Still, both candidates’ cases for victory are pretty easy to craft. Let’s start with the case for why Talarico is going to win:

President Trump is historically unpopular. Gasoline prices are high and diesel prices are through the roof, which is going to hurt Trump in a state with many long-haul drivers and pickup trucks. The president won Texas by 14 points in 2024, supported in large part by the Latino vote and anti-Kamala Harris sentiment. Now, Latinos are shifting back to the left, Democrats have a much stronger candidate on the ballot and we’re in a midterm election, which historically hurts the incumbent party. The closest analogue here might be the 2018 midterm race, when Trump was in office and O’Rourke came within 2.6 points of flipping Ted Cruz’s Senate seat, despite polls showing him much further behind. These races come down to turnout, and Democrats seem much more committed to voting than Republicans do this election season. 

Speaking of Republicans, Ken Paxton is a disaster. He’s a comically corrupt (alleged) adulterer, in a national environment where voters say corruption is their number-one issue and in a state where traditional marital values are popular. Leaks from Paxton’s campaign portray a candidate who knows Trump is hurting him and can’t find his footing on the trail.

On paper, all the momentum and evidence look good for Talarico. While O’Rourke made noise, he never led a single poll; Talarico has had an advantage in the polls since August and is running in a much more favorable environment. Plus, the concocted conspiracy theory that Talarico was checked into a mental health facility reeks of desperation. If it weren’t for Elon Musk floating Paxton’s campaign, Talarico’s historic fundraising numbers would be a giant advantage and a huge story. In southwest Texas, the administration’s attempt to build a border wall in the Big Bend region and National Park is activating huge blowback from a bipartisan coalition of politicians, ranchers, hunters, river guides, small business owners, and even law enforcement. And while Trump accused Talarico of avoiding a debate, the reality is Talarico’s campaign has repeatedly tried to organize a debate with Paxton, and Paxton keeps dodging him — so much so that Talarico ended up doing a solo town hall with Texas voters that was aired on CNN last Wednesday. 

Anecdotally, I’d add that Talarico’s campaign has a tremendous amount of enthusiasm among Democrats in Texas. I live in New Jersey full time but own property in West Texas, where I spent my summers growing up and now spend a lot of my winters. I’ve never felt anything like the current political momentum there, and it’s all going in one direction: an all-out effort to oust Gov. Greg Abbott (R), stop Ken Paxton, and rein in President Trump.

For Democrats, that all sounds pretty exciting. But the case for Paxton is still compelling.

At baseline, Texas is a red state. The state doesn’t collect party registration data, but Trump’s decisive victory in 2024 is one of the best measures of how voters break in statewide elections. A recent YouGov survey has 41% of likely voters in Texas identifying as Republican, 26% as Democrat, and 28% as independent — close, but still a healthy Republican advantage. 

Meanwhile, the core issues that are driving Trump’s unpopularity — the war in Iran, affordability, and the immigration crackdown — are all softened in Texas. Yes, diesel prices are high nationally, and Texas has faced its own economic emergency over those costs. But unlike other states, Texas also has an upside from the war: Its oil production is thriving, meaning Texas producers can charge more, juice profits, and provide a lot of jobs. Trump’s nationally unpopular mass-deportation effort has a lot of support in Texas. And Trump, who is still good at turning out his base, has spent a lot of political capital throwing his weight behind Paxton.

And then there’s Musk. With nearly $160 million spent already, he’s single-handedly funding super PACs that are blanketing the state in pro-Paxton or anti-Talarico ads. And, if you watched the CNN town hall, voters were more focused on Talarico’s progressive social views (some from as recently as 2020 and 2021) than on his populist left economic views, which is a problem for his campaign. We’ve seen that focus on progressive social views work for the GOP before, and Republican groups are even running the same “He is for they/them” ad against Talarico that was famously effective against Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race. As I detailed in my latest YouTube video, fear is a powerful and effective campaign strategy, one Texas Republicans are deploying to a much higher degree than Talarico in this cycle (they even have AI-generated ads of Talarico defacing a Bible).

Finally, the “closeness” of the race could be a total mirage, anyway. In 2024, polling showed Trump with a roughly seven-point lead and he won by 14. In that year’s Senate race, polls showed Cruz up about four points on Colin Allred; he won by over eight points. In the 2022 governor’s race, Abbott led O’Rourke by an average of eight points; he won by about 11. 

Which is all just to say that the polling may be tight (and point to a Talarico advantage), but I have less confidence in current polls than I have in a long time. I’m holding off on any midterm predictions until we get closer to Election Day, but this race obviously has the potential to tilt the Senate map — and make Texas history. 

Take the survey: Who do you think will win the election? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The Russia diesel deal.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, a look back at Justice Clarence Thomas’s confirmation.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Russia diesel deal. On Friday, President Donald Trump announced an agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports in return for Russia releasing roughly 800,000 tons of diesel by the end of November and millions more by an unspecified date. The president said the deal will bring down diesel prices impacted by supply disruptions linked to the Iran war but did not say it is tied to a larger ceasefire deal. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and some U.S. lawmakers criticized the agreement as a gift to Russia and urged Trump to reverse course. 

Back up: In response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the U.S. and other Western countries leveled broad sanctions on the Russian economy and individual leaders. In September, Congress passed a new set of sanctions — some of which applied to Russia’s energy sector — with strong bipartisan support, and President Trump signed the bill into law. 

Under the announced terms, the U.S. will temporarily remove sanctions on Russian diesel exports, and Russia will immediately supply the U.S. and global marketplace with approximately 300,000 metric tons of the fuel. They’ll supply another 500,000 tons in November and an additional one million tons “immediately thereafter,” according to Trump. The president also said Russia will supply three million additional tons “within a short period of time” based on Russian refinery capabilities. 

President Zelensky immediately spoke out against the deal, saying, “It looks like a happy birthday present for Putin… It shows weakness of the world.” Zelensky also suggested that a U.S. negotiating team had misled Ukrainian officials about Trump’s discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the energy agreement. Other Western leaders also questioned the deal; Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said, “It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue ​to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions.”

Separately, on Sunday, President Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia, saying, “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” However, Zelensky indicated that he was not aware of an agreement or the terms of the purported ceasefire, later accusing Russia of attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. 

On Tuesday, a group of six Democratic and six Republican senators sent a letter to Trump asking him to back out of the diesel deal. “[The agreement] will have a negligible impact on fuel prices but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance security cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea,” they wrote. 

Today, we’ll share perspectives from the left and right on the deal, followed by Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left opposes the deal, with some saying it won’t bring down energy prices.
  • Many expect Russia’s war effort will benefit. 
  • Others suggest Trump is selling out Ukraine.

The Guardian editorial board wrote about the “imperative to keep pump prices down.”

“Mr. Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections,” the board said. “The real driver of global energy prices is not Ukraine defending itself from Russian attack, but Mr. Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. 

“Blaming Mr. Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled,” the board wrote. “The best response to Mr. Trump’s perfidy is for Mr. Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support… thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.”

In The Philadelphia Inquirer, Trudy Rubin suggested the deal will “fund Putin’s war machine.”

“The ‘diesel deal’ Trump has gifted Putin won’t halt Russia’s aggression. It will reward it,” Rubin wrote. “It will encourage the Kremlin’s unyielding demand that Kyiv surrender to Moscow’s overlordship. And it will fuel Putin’s war chest… The Ukrainians were ready to discuss a two-way ceasefire over attacks on energy infrastructure, but were totally blindsided. Instead, Trump unilaterally declared such a ceasefire had been reached. It hadn’t.”

“Yet when Zelensky rejected the one-sided diesel deal, Trump went ballistic and called for his replacement, as if Ukraine were a banana republic whose president could be ousted overnight,” Rubin said. “If Putin keeps getting freebies from his friend Donald, why make concessions? Lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as Zelensky noted, not only gives Putin ‘more money to inflict suffering on us’ but ‘gives him the ability to fight even more.’”

In The Atlantic, Anne Applebaum said “Donald Trump has dropped all pretense.”

“[President Trump] lifted sanctions on the import of Russian diesel fuel, in violation of the letter and spirit of laws that he himself signed,” Applebaum wrote. “The president has implied that the point of his new policy is to lower fuel prices for Americans. But this is not a sufficient explanation or justification for these dramatic actions. The amount of fuel that Russia could export is too small, the impact on pricing too slight, the narrative too late to shape electoral outcomes. 

“This looks, instead, like something very different: an abrupt, Hail Mary attempt to force Ukraine to surrender and to save the Russian economy, perhaps in order to finally complete the multiple business deals that the Russians are known to have discussed with American negotiators and others in Trump’s orbit,” Applebaum said. “American allies in Europe and elsewhere have tried to explain to the president the significance of the war and the threat that Russia poses... Now it looks as if they have failed, and Trump has followed his oldest instincts to side with Putin.”

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with some calling the deal a strong strategic move. 
  • Others argue that the agreement is a short-term solution to a long-term problem.
  • Still others contend Trump’s deal supports Putin’s war efforts.

In Fox News, Gordon Sondland suggested Trump is “threading the needle.”

“Europe is not yet strong enough to contain Russia without substantial American support. Despite years of promises, too many NATO allies remain dependent on American military capabilities, intelligence, logistics and leadership,” Sondland wrote. “Every additional weapons system, dollar and hour of strategic attention consumed by Moscow is a resource unavailable for deterring Beijing or addressing other threats… Trump is trying to change that equation. 

“In the long run, we want a fully economically engaged Russia that has something meaningful to lose,” Sondland said. “That doesn’t mean trusting Putin. It means understanding his incentives. Putin wants two things: money and real estate. He wants the economic benefits of international engagement and the territorial advantages of an empire. Trump is uniquely positioned to offer the former while making the latter prohibitively expensive. That is the needle Trump is trying to thread.”

In the Daily Caller, David Blackmon wrote about energy’s “long-term problem.”

“Any visible relief at the pump before the mid-terms would matter politically as well as economically,” Blackmon wrote. “But, with just three weeks until Election Day… the same constraints remain: Utilization rates that are not sustainable, thin inventories, and the absence of new domestic refining capacity. Temporary imports and sanctions waivers can buy time, but they do not substitute for permitting and building additional domestic capacity. 

“If the new diesel flows and the energy truce are kept, U.S. consumers will no doubt see some price relief. If any of the deal’s fundamentals fail, the pressure on U.S. refineries continues unabated,” Blackmon said. “Either outcome leaves the central problem intact: The U.S. and the world need more refining capacity than current policies and geopolitics have allowed, and two ongoing wars have robbed markets of all their cushions. Something has got to give.”

The Wall Street Journal editorial board said the deal will “directly finance Mr. Putin’s bloody war.”

“The Financial Times reported Saturday that the Trump Administration ‘threatened to cut off vital intelligence sharing’ to Kyiv if it continues attacking Russian refineries,” the board wrote. “On Wednesday 22 people, including five children, were killed in a Russian cruise missile strike on an apartment building… After the diesel announcement, Russia launched glide bombs Saturday at a residential area of Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 20.”

“Without a complete cease-fire, Russia will continue to torment Ukrainian civilians. The strategic turn here is hard to understand,” the board said. “[Trump’s] multiple attempts at appeasing Mr. Putin… haven’t moved the Russian. On the weekend a Russian official said the diesel deal doesn’t change Mr. Putin’s determination to achieve his war aim, which is to turn Ukraine into a Kremlin satrapy. Until that changes, Mr. Trump’s diesel deal helps Russia and not the cause of peace.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • From President Trump’s standpoint, a deal with Russia could offer a chance to alleviate fuel prices ahead of the midterms.
  • From Putin’s standpoint, Trump is offering major economic relief during a war of attrition with Ukraine.
  • This deal reeks of desperation; it hurts our allies, helps our enemies, won’t lower gas prices, and is probably illegal.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Imagine you are in President Trump’s position. 

At the urging of a Middle East ally, you’ve led the nation into a conflict with Iran that has proved much more difficult to end than you imagined. Iranian forces have been able to disrupt (or, at times, completely shut down) the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for oil shipping, something you may have known was possible but never imagined would be so difficult to resolve. Bravado and bombs have not freed up the waterway, nor have quieter tactical negotiations or special operations. As the midterms have inched closer, fuel prices have continued to rise, driving persistent inflation. Despite leading a country that dominates diesel exports, diesel prices have also skyrocketed to the detriment of Americans.

At the same time, you haven’t been able to negotiate a truce between Ukraine and Russia, which you promised you’d do in the first 24 hours of your presidency. Vladimir Putin is an influential, authoritarian leader you harbor a kind of twisted respect for, while Volodymyr Zelensky is a petulant, persistent leader of a less significant country who desperately needs your support but has less to offer in return. You thought Putin would defeat Zelensky, then briefly thought Zelensky would defeat Putin, and now fear that the effective Ukrainian strategy of targeting Russian oil refineries will further disrupt an already fragile global energy supply. And, still, the midterms inch closer.

So you have a predicament. Expensive foreign diesel is not necessarily bad for U.S. producers. In theory, they should benefit from the short supply by making more money refining crude oil into diesel. However, American consumers pay the downstream costs of more expensive diesel: From freight companies paying higher transportation costs to your average Great Plains rancher getting crushed at the pump, the bad outweighs the good. These pains are felt globally, and a lot of world leaders blame you, since you launched a war with Iran, which also disrupted global energy supply. You could definitely use a scapegoat.

The obvious solution to lower prices is to create more supply, and the simplest route is to free up the Strait of Hormuz, allowing more diesel to flow in every direction and bringing down the costs globally. But you have not been able to get the strait back to “normal,” and after several attempts you start to look at the rest of your board: You’ve played your hand in Venezuela, you’ve made major releases from the strategic U.S. oil reserve — that leaves Russia.

Now imagine being in Vladimir Putin’s position: You invaded Ukraine in 2022, plunging Eastern Europe into disarray and sending an economic and energy shock across the globe. When the war started, you were exporting about 40 million tons of diesel per year. The United Kingdom and Europe tried to punish you by not buying your diesel, so you replaced their markets with countries like Turkey, Brazil, and nations across Africa. This worked for a while, and as of April this year, you still had some 3 million tons of diesel per month available to export, or 36 million tons per year.

And then Ukraine opened up a new front in the war. They started bombing your oil refineries, and by September, your export rate was decimated — down to 325,000 tons per month. To avoid a domestic shortage, you banned diesel exports everywhere except Central Asia and Mongolia. You’re weathering the storm, refusing a ceasefire with Ukraine and escalating the war there, hoping that your country can pace its own use of oil to stave off economic calamity until well after Ukraine’s financial ruin.

In walks President Trump. He’s got an offer: Export a few million tons of diesel between now and April 2027, and over that period he will suspend the economic sanctions he has in place to punish anyone buying diesel from you — no strings attached to a ceasefire or peace deal with Ukraine. The diesel you’ll export in the arrangement is worth about $7 billion, and with the sanctions gone, you won’t have to sell it at a discount. For the U.S., this will create more supply in the global system, theoretically bringing down global oil and diesel prices.

There’s your deal.

As for the millions of us American voters and consumers, I have a few frameworks for thinking about this deal: First, is it good for America? According to Reuters, Russia is going to immediately supply 300,000 metric tons (or 2.25 million barrels) of diesel to the United States and global markets. That sounds like an astronomical amount, and I suppose it is. But it’s less than a day’s supply for the U.S. transport sector alone, and it’s going to be dispersed globally. Trump has said Russia will release another 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million after that, which altogether amounts to about four days of the total diesel demand for U.S. transport. 

The Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center suggested the deal might bring prices down marginally, but many market players have already factored in assumptions that Russia would export all the surplus diesel it could — it has no place to store it otherwise. Real price relief would only come if Kyiv stopped bombing Russian refineries, which it isn’t going to do, since it has learned that’s a powerful lever to pull.

And that’s just the benefits. The costs — benefiting a geopolitical rival, undermining a geopolitical ally, and embroiling the U.S. government in yet another questionable international deal — are also real.

That brings me to my second framework: Is President Trump’s deal even legal? The sanctions statute was enacted in 2022 under President Biden. While presidents typically have broad authority to waive sanctions, this specific law was unusual, putting in plain text that the president must first consult with several congressional committees, submit a report 45 days before making changes, and provide certification to Congress before lifting the prohibition. In fact, the entire sanctions relief — by law — is dependent on Russia withdrawing from Ukraine and ceasing hostilities, a determination that must be accepted by Ukraine. None of that has happened, so many legal experts and a bipartisan coalition of Congress say the president broke the law, and they have called for the president to rescind the deal.

Third, and finally, is the larger geopolitical context: Will this meaningfully address the global energy crisis? Remember, Russia’s war didn’t spark the 2026 global energy crisis — Trump’s decision to attack Iran did. The deal itself won’t be much of an economic boon for Russia (the $7 billion of diesel was going to be sold anyway, and at just slightly cheaper rates), but the signal it sends is helpful for Putin. It comes at a time when Ukraine is accusing the U.S. of hampering its battlefield tech and halting shared intelligence about Russian attacks. In sum, we appear to be turning on Ukraine, handing a small but meaningful economic gift to Putin, and doing it all for an uncertain and marginal improvement in energy prices — prices that were destabilized by a different war that we started. 

Oh, and this is all happening a month after the president signed a bipartisan bill that explicitly leveled sanctions and tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. Trump explained the sudden pivot by saying his number one priority was ranchers, farmers and truckers, and he blamed Ukraine for ignoring requests to stop bombing Russian refineries.

It’s a mess — a genuine election-time Hail Mary that could have long-term negative implications for our international relations (after all, we’ve been punishing countries for buying Russian oil until now) and for the future of Ukraine (which is suddenly dealt yet another disadvantage in the war). I’m open to arguments that this is somehow “good” for us, or the global geopolitical situation, but I’ve seen very little in the way of compelling points to that end. 

Take the survey: Do you think the deal will affect energy prices? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.
